concepts.title: Coring Function
concepts.one_liner: A coring function modifies noisy observations by setting coefficient values near zero to zero, based on the high prior probability of zero values.
concepts.content:
A coring function is used to modify a noisy observation to reach the MAP estimate for a denoised coefficient value. If a coefficient value is observed near zero, it is set to zero, based on the very high prior probability of zero coefficient values.

(see figure: Input/output coring curve for maximum posterior denoising for the example of @fig-waveletBayes)
concepts.motivation_md: In denoising, small coefficient values are often more likely to be noise than signal. Coring leverages the statistical prior that many natural image coefficients are zero to suppress this noise.
concepts.recap_md:
- Sets coefficient values near zero to exactly zero.
 - Implements a Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimate for denoising.

concepts.title: Markov Random Field (MRF) Models

position.section_title: Nonparametric Markov Random Field Image Models

concepts.one_liner: Markov random field (MRF) models assume a pixel's probability distribution is independent of the rest of the image if enough surrounding pixels are specified.
concepts.content: Markov random field (MRF) models are a powerful class of image models. The core intuition for these models is that if the values of enough pixels surrounding a given pixel are specified, then the probability distribution of the given pixel is independent of the other pixels in the image. To fit and sample from the MRF structure requires the mathematical tools of graphical models. This Markov structure can be exploited to synthesize textures that are visually compelling.
concepts.motivation_md: MRFs provide a mathematically precise way to model local dependencies in images, allowing for complex global structures to emerge from simple local rules.
concepts.recap_md:
- Assumes local pixel neighborhoods determine a pixel's probability distribution.
 - Requires graphical model tools for fitting and sampling.

 - Requires graphical model tools for fitting and sampling.

concepts.title: Efros and Leung Texture Synthesis

position.section_title: Nonparametric Markov Random Field Image Models

concepts.one_liner: The Efros and Leung algorithm synthesizes textures by conditioning the value of a central pixel on a large enough region of nearby pixels.
concepts.content: Efros and Leung introduced an algorithm for texture synthesis that exploits intuitions about the Markov structure of images to synthesize textures that are visually compelling. The intuition of the Efros and Leung texture generation model is that if you condition on a large enough region of nearby pixels around a center pixel, that effectively determines the value of the central pixel.
concepts.motivation_md: This technique solves the problem of generating new texture samples that look like a given example by assuming that local neighborhoods contain enough information to predict missing pixels.
concepts.recap_md:
- Exploits Markov structure for texture generation.
 - Determines central pixel values based on surrounding local regions.

concepts.title: Nonlocal Means Denoising

position.section_title: Nonparametric Markov Random Field Image Models

concepts.one_liner: Nonlocal means denoising computes a pixel's value as a weighted sum of all other pixels, weighted by the similarity of their local neighborhoods.
concepts.content:
The nonlocal means denoising algorithm defines the denoised image as a weighted sum of all other pixels in the image, weighted by the similarity of the local neighborhoods of each pair of pixels. More formally,
$$\ell_{\mbox{NLM}}[n,m] = \sum_{k,l} w_{n,m}[k,l] \ell[k,l]$$ where
$$w_{n,m}[k,l] = \frac{1}{Z_{n,m}} \exp{\frac{- \left| \ell[N_{k,l}] - ℓ[N_{n,m}] \right| ^2}{h^2}},$$
where $N_{i, j}$ denotes an $h \times h$ region of pixels centered at $i, j$, and $Z_{n,m}$ is set so that the weights over the image sum to one, that is $\sum_{kl} w_{n,m}[k,l] = 1$.

(see figure: Nonlocal means denoising algorithm results. (left) Original image without noise. (middle) Noisy image. (right) Denoised image.*Source*:Figure from @Baudes2011)
concepts.motivation_md: Standard filters only look at nearby pixels; nonlocal means recognizes that similar patterns (like a texture or edge) may recur far away in the image and uses them to improve the denoising estimate.
concepts.recap_md:
- Denoises by averaging pixels with similar local neighborhoods.
 - Uses a global weighted sum where weights depend on patch similarity.

slots.motivation: Standard filters only look at nearby pixels; nonlocal means recognizes that similar patterns (like a texture or edge) may recur far away in the image and uses them to improve the denoising estimate.
slots.key_passage:
- Denoises by averaging pixels with similar local neighborhoods.
 - Uses a global weighted sum where weights depend on patch similarity.

concepts.title: Nonlocal Means Weighting Functions

position.section_title: Nonparametric Markov Random Field Image Models

concepts.one_liner: The weighting function in nonlocal means determines which pixels are averaged together based on the similarity of their local structures to the target pixel.
concepts.content:
The weighting function $w_{n,m}[k,l]$ indicates which pixels are averaged together to yield the nonlocal mean value placed at a specific location in the denoised image. The parameter $h$ is typically set to $10 \sigma$, where $\sigma$ is the estimated image noise standard deviation. Sampling occurs at image regions with similar local structure as the image position to be denoised.

[FIGURE:c5b8102b308188df | Four square panels demonstrating the Non-Local Means weighting function. The first pair shows a brick wall texture with a white dot at the center; its corresponding weight map shows a grid of white...]
concepts.motivation_md: Defining weights based on neighborhood similarity allows the algorithm to preserve sharp edges and repetitive textures that simple spatial blurring would destroy.
concepts.recap_md:
- Weights are determined by the similarity of $h \times h$ pixel regions.
 - The parameter $h$ is usually scaled relative to the noise standard deviation $\sigma$.

concepts.title: Statistical Image Regularities
concepts.one_liner: Statistical image models utilize low-level regularities to constrain the space of natural images for tasks like synthesis and denoising.
concepts.content:
Statistical image models utilize low-level regularities of images in order to build a statistical model without trying to understand the content of the pictures. Modeling these statistical regularities enables many tasks, including both image synthesis and image denoising. While these models help constrain the space of natural images, simple models often fail to provide a strong enough model to sample entirely new, realistic images, as the space of natural images is a very small part of the space of all possible images.

(see figure: The space of natural images is just very small part of the space of all possible images. In the case of color images with $32 \times 32$ pixels, most of the space is filled with images that look like...)
concepts.motivation_md: By identifying patterns common to almost all natural images (like smoothness or edge statistics), we can distinguish signal from noise and generate realistic textures.
concepts.recap_md:
- Uses low-level patterns rather than high-level semantic understanding.
 - Helps reduce the search space from all possible images to 'natural' images.

concepts.title: Definition of Natural Image
concepts.one_liner: A natural image is a sample from the relatively small subset of all possible pixel arrays that represent real-world visual scenes.
concepts.content: An image is a very high dimensional array of pixels $\ell\left[n,m\right]$. The space of all possible images is extremely large; for example, even $32\times32$ pixel thumbnails with three color channels and 8 bits per channel result in more than $10^{7,398}$ possible images. Most of these possible images consist of random noise. Natural images occupy only a very small part of this total space. (see figure: The space of natural images is just very small part of the space of all possible images. In the case of color images with $32\times32$ pixels, most of the space is filled with images that look like...) A typical sample from the set of all images consists of pixels independently sampled from a uniform distribution, whereas natural images possess specific structures and properties.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding that natural images occupy a tiny manifold within the space of all possible pixel combinations is fundamental for developing effective compression, denoising, and generative models.
concepts.recap_md: - Natural images are a tiny subset of the high-dimensional space of all possible pixel arrays.

concepts.title: Visual Worlds
concepts.one_liner: Visual worlds are simplified image sets used to characterize specific properties of natural images through analytic tools and generative models.
concepts.content: As natural images are complex, researchers use simple visual worlds that retain important properties of natural images while allowing for analytic characterization. These worlds range from white noise and Gabor patches to CGI and real street scenes. (see figure: Different visual worlds, some real, some synthetic. (a) White noise. (b) Gabor patches. (c) Mondrian. (d) Stars. (e) Clouds. (f) Line drawing. (g) Computer graphic imagery (CGI). (h) A real street...) Each world has unique visual characteristics that can be captured by specific models. These models help in understanding what makes the set of real images unique and can be applied to tasks like noise removal, predicting missing high-frequencies, and filling in occluded regions.
concepts.motivation_md: By studying simplified synthetic environments, researchers can isolate and model specific visual phenomena before tackling the full complexity of the natural world.
concepts.recap_md: - Visual worlds are simplified sets of images used to study specific visual characteristics.

concepts.title: Differentiating Noise from Texture

position.section_title: How Do We Tell Noise from Texture?

concepts.one_liner: Differentiating noise from texture involves determining if a pattern is an independent corruption of the image or an intrinsic property of a 3D surface.
concepts.content: (see figure: Telling noise from surface texture. Which one is which?) Stationary image noise is an independent process from the image content. It is not affected by object boundaries, does not deform according to the 3D orientation of surfaces, and does not change frequency with distance from the camera. In contrast, a surface texture is part of the world; if noise were truly in the world, it would have to conspire with the observer's viewpoint to appear stationary. [FIGURE:680c813998d8644a | @fig-noiseInTheWorld (b) has noise added] Image denoising relies on this distinction, aiming to separate an image into a clean component and a noise component based on statistical models.
concepts.motivation_md: Distinguishing between sensor noise and physical surface patterns is crucial for image restoration and for understanding how the human visual system interprets scene content.
concepts.recap_md: - Stationary noise is independent of scene content and geometry, unlike surface textures.

concepts.title: Additive Stationary Noise

position.section_title: How Do We Tell Noise from Texture?

concepts.one_liner: Additive stationary noise is noise with statistical properties independent of location that is added to an observation.
concepts.content: Additive stationary noise is defined as noise whose statistical properties are independent of its spatial location within an image. This noise is added to the underlying clean observation. A more precise mathematical treatment of this concept can be found in the context of Gaussian image denoising models.
concepts.motivation_md: This model provides a mathematically tractable way to represent common types of electronic or sensor interference in image acquisition.
concepts.recap_md: - Stationary noise has statistical properties that do not change across different image locations.

concepts.title: Procedural vs. Statistical Image Models

position.section_title: How Do We Tell Noise from Texture?

concepts.one_liner: Image models can be built either through procedural descriptions like rendering engines or through statistical models that capture local neighborhood properties.
concepts.content: There are two primary ways to build image models that represent the uniqueness of real photographs. The first is a procedural description, which uses a list of objects, poses, and styles combined with a rendering engine (similar to CGI). However, this requires an exhaustive list of everything in the world. The second approach is building statistical models of images. These models attempt to capture the properties of small image neighborhoods, starting from the simplest case of a single pixel. Statistical models are foundational in fields like natural language modeling and offer a way to handle the complexity of the visual world without explicit procedural lists.
concepts.motivation_md: Choosing between procedural and statistical modeling allows researchers to balance explicit scene knowledge against the ability to learn patterns directly from data.
concepts.recap_md: - Procedural models use rendering rules, while statistical models use probability distributions of pixels.

concepts.title: Independent Pixel Model
concepts.one_liner: The independent pixel model assumes all pixels are independent and their intensities are drawn from a stationary distribution.
concepts.content: The simplest image model assumes that all pixels are independent and their intensity values are drawn from a stationary distribution, meaning the distribution is independent of the pixel's location. The probability $p_{\theta}(\boldsymbol\ell)$ of an image $\ell[n,m]$ of size $N \times M$ is given by: $$p_{\theta}(\boldsymbol\ell) = \prod_{n=1}^{N} \prod_{m=1}^{M} p_{\theta}\left(\ell[n,m] \right)$$ Here, $p_{\theta}$ denotes a parameterized probability model where the vector $\theta$ contains parameters that can be fitted to data using maximum likelihood or other loss functions.
concepts.motivation_md: This model serves as a baseline for image analysis, demonstrating the limitations of ignoring spatial correlations between neighboring pixels.
concepts.recap_md: - Assumes every pixel's value is independent of its neighbors.

slots.motivation: This model serves as a baseline for image analysis, demonstrating the limitations of ignoring spatial correlations between neighboring pixels.
slots.key_passage: - Assumes every pixel's value is independent of its neighbors.

The probability $p_{\theta}(\boldsymbol\ell)$ of an image $\ell[n,m]$ of size $N \times M$ is given by: $$p_{\theta}(\boldsymbol\ell) = \prod_{n=1}^{N} \prod_{m=1}^{M} p_{\theta}\left(\ell[n,m] \right)$$ Here, $p_{\theta}$ denotes a parameterized probability model where the vector $\theta$ contains parameters that can be fitted to data using maximum likelihood or other loss functions.

concepts.title: Sampling from a Statistical Image Model
concepts.one_liner: Sampling from a statistical image model involves generating new images based on a learned probability distribution to assess the model's accuracy.
concepts.content: One way to assess a statistical image model is to sample from it and view the resulting images. This requires knowing the distribution $p_{\theta}\left(\ell[n,m] \right)$. For a discrete gray-scale image with 256 levels, $p_{\theta}$ is a vector of 256 values; for color images, it involves $256^3$ bins. (see figure: Fitting a statistical image model to a set of training images. Once the model is learned we can use the model to sample new images.) The parameters $\theta$ can be estimated as the average histogram of a training set or a single image. To sample a new image, each pixel is sampled independently using the intensity distribution. (see figure: Estimation of the image model parameters using one image, and then sampling a new image by sampling pixels independently using the histogram of the training image.) In the multinomial model, the probability of a pixel at $(n,m)$ having value $k$ is $p_{\theta}(\ell [n,m] = k) = \theta_k$. (see figure: Examples of images and corresponding random samples with the same distribution of pixel intensities. Only the image with stars (a) has some visual similarity with the randomly sampled image.) While this works for simple cases like star fields, it fails for complex images because treating pixels as independent observations ignores the inherent structure of images.
concepts.motivation_md: Sampling allows for a qualitative visual inspection of what a statistical model has actually learned, revealing whether it captures the essential structures of the target data.
concepts.recap_md: - New images are generated by sampling each pixel independently from a learned histogram.

concepts.title: Histogram Matching
concepts.one_liner: Histogram matching is a pixelwise transformation that modifies an image so its intensity distribution matches the histogram of another image.
concepts.content: Manipulating image histograms is a very useful operation. Given two images $\boldsymbol\ell_1$ and $\boldsymbol\ell_2$ with histograms $\mathbf{h}_1$ and $\mathbf{h}_2$, we look for a pixelwise transformation $f\left(\ell[n,m] \right)$ so that the histogram of the transformed image, $f\left(\ell_1 [n,m] \right)$, matches the histogram of $\boldsymbol\ell_2$. There are many ways in which histograms can be transformed. One natural choice is a transformation that preserves the ordering of pixels intensities.
concepts.motivation_md: While simple histogram models are poor generative models for creating realistic images, histogram manipulation is a powerful tool for image processing and adjusting visual characteristics.
concepts.recap_md:
- It seeks a pixelwise function $f$ to align the intensity distribution of one image with another.
- A common approach is to use transformations that preserve the original ordering of pixel intensities.

slots.motivation: While simple histogram models are poor generative models for creating realistic images, histogram manipulation is a powerful tool for image processing and adjusting visual characteristics.
slots.key_passage:

- A common approach is to use transformations that preserve the original ordering of pixel intensities.

concepts.title: Perceptual Importance of Histogram Manipulations
concepts.one_liner: Simple histogram manipulations can significantly alter the perceived material properties of objects, such as changing a surface from shiny to matte.
concepts.content:
The perceptual importance of simple histogram manipulations can be illustrated by spheres reflecting complex ambient illumination. By simply changing the image histogram, we can transform how we perceive the material of each sphere: from shiny to matte. For example, a sphere rendered with illumination from a campus photograph or from pink noise (random noise with a $\frac{1}{|w_x^2+w_y^2|}$ power spectrum) can have its histogram swapped with another. Modifying the image histograms within the pixels of the sphere creates a different sense of gloss, making the sphere appear to be made of a different type of material.

(see figure: Perceptual importance of simple histogram manipulations. Figure from @Fleming2001)
concepts.motivation_md: This concept demonstrates that low-level statistical properties like histograms are crucial for high-level visual tasks like material perception.
concepts.recap_md:
- Histogram swapping can change the perceived gloss or material of a rendered object.
- These manipulations show that material perception is tied to the distribution of pixel intensities.

concepts.title: Pixel Correlation Function
concepts.one_liner: The pixel correlation function measures the statistical relationship between the intensities of two pixels as a function of their spatial separation.
concepts.content:
In the quest to find what makes photographs of everyday scenes special, the next simplest image structure is a set of two pixels. If one plots the value of the intensity of one pixel as a function of the intensity value of a nearby pixel, the scatterplot is concentrated on the identity line. As we look at the correlation between pixels that are farther away, the correlation value slowly decays. The correlation, $C$, between two pixels separated by offsets of $\Delta n$ and $\Delta m$, is:
$$C(\Delta n, \Delta m) = \rho \left( \ell[n+\Delta n,m+ \Delta m], \ell[n,m] \right)$$
where
$$\rho \left( a, b \right) = \frac{E \left( (a-\bar{a})( b- \bar{b}) \right)}{\sigma_a \sigma_b},$$
and $\sigma_a$ is the standard deviation of the variable $a$, and $\bar{a}$ is the mean of $a$.

(see figure: (center) Scatter plots of pairs of pixels intensities as a function of distance and (right) cross-correlation as a function for vertical (green) and horizontal (red) displacements for the street...)
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the statistical dependencies between neighboring pixels is a fundamental step in modeling the structure of natural images.
concepts.recap_md:
- Pixel intensities in natural images are highly correlated with their neighbors.
- This correlation typically decays as the spatial distance between pixels increases.

slots.motivation: Understanding the statistical dependencies between neighboring pixels is a fundamental step in modeling the structure of natural images.
slots.key_passage:
- Pixel intensities in natural images are highly correlated with their neighbors.
- This correlation typically decays as the spatial distance between pixels increases.

In the quest to find what makes photographs of everyday scenes special, the next simplest image structure is a set of two pixels. If one plots the value of the intensity of one pixel as a function of the intensity value of a nearby pixel, the scatterplot is concentrated on the identity line. As we look at the correlation between pixels that are farther away, the correlation value slowly decays. The correlation, $C$, between two pixels separated by offsets of $\Delta n$ and $\Delta m$, is:
$$C(\Delta n, \Delta m) = \rho \left( \ell[n+\Delta n,m+ \Delta m], \ell[n,m] \right)$$
where
$$\rho \left( a, b \right) = \frac{E \left( (a-\bar{a})( b- \bar{b}) \right)}{\sigma_a \sigma_b},$$
and $\sigma_a$ is the standard deviation of the variable $a$, and $\bar{a}$ is the mean of $a$.

(see figure: (center) Scatter plots of pairs of pixels intensities as a function of distance and (right) cross-correlation as a function for vertical (green) and horizontal (red) displacements for the street...)

concepts.title: Gaussian Image Model
concepts.one_liner: The Gaussian image model is a maximum entropy statistical model that accounts for the correlation and power spectrum of natural images.
concepts.content:
(see figure: (center) Scatter plots of pairs of pixels intensities as a function of distance and (right) cross-correlation as a function for vertical (green) and horizontal (red) displacements for the street...)

A statistical image model can be constructed to account for the correlation statistics and the power spectrum of natural images. If the only constraint is the correlation function among pixels, the maximum entropy distribution is the Gaussian distribution:
$$p(\boldsymbol\ell) \propto \exp \left(-\frac{1}{2} \boldsymbol\ell^\mathsf{T}{\bf C}^{-1} \boldsymbol\ell\right)$$
where ${\bf C}$ is the covariance matrix of all image pixels. This model accounts for the correlation of intensity values between different pixels rather than assuming independence.

For stationary signals, the covariance matrix ${\bf C}$ has a circulant structure and can be diagonalized using the Fourier transform: ${\bf C} = {\bf F}{\bf D}{\bf F}^\mathsf{T}$. Here, ${\bf F}$ contains the Fourier basis and the diagonal matrix ${\bf D}$ contains values $1/ w ^\alpha$ for all radial frequencies $w$, where $\alpha$ is typically set to 1.5.
concepts.motivation_md: The Gaussian model provides a mathematically tractable way to capture the primary spatial correlations found in natural scenes using the principle of maximum entropy.
concepts.recap_md:
- It models image probability using a Gaussian distribution based on a pixel covariance matrix.
- The covariance matrix is often diagonalized in the Fourier domain using a power-law decay.

concepts.title: Dead Leaves Model
concepts.one_liner: The dead leaves model is a simplified image formation model that represents an image as a random superposition of overlapping shapes.
concepts.content:
The dead leaves model is a simplified image formation model that tries to approximate some of the properties observed for natural images. Introduced by Matheron in the 1960s and popularized by Ruderman in the 1990s, the model is best described by a procedure: an image is modeled as a set of shapes (dead leaves) that fall on a flat surface, generating a random superposition.

![Images sampled from the dead leaves model, for different shapes of dead leaves. (a) Circles, and (b) Squares. ](figures/statistical_image_models/dead_leaves_squares_and_circles.png){width="100%" #fig-deadleaves}
concepts.motivation_md: This model provides a more realistic approximation of natural image properties, such as occlusion and edges, compared to simpler noise models.
concepts.recap_md:
- It simulates image creation by randomly dropping and overlapping geometric shapes.
- It captures key structural properties of natural images like occlusion.

concepts.title: Power Spectrum
concepts.one_liner: The power spectrum of a signal is defined as the square of the magnitude of its Fourier transform.
concepts.content: The Fourier transform of the autocorrelation of a signal is the square of the magnitude of its Fourier Transform. The square of the magnitude of the FT, $\lVert \mathscr{L}(u,v) \rVert ^2$, is the power spectrum of a signal.
concepts.motivation_md: The power spectrum is a fundamental tool for analyzing the frequency content and energy distribution of signals and images.
concepts.recap_md:
- It is the squared magnitude of the Fourier transform: $\lVert \mathscr{L}(u,v) \rVert ^2$.
- It is mathematically equivalent to the Fourier transform of the signal's autocorrelation.

concepts.title: Power Law of Natural Images
concepts.one_liner: The magnitude of the Fourier transform of most natural images follows a power law, falling off as $1/w^\alpha$ with frequency.
concepts.content:
One remarkable property of most natural images is that if you take the 2D Fourier transform of an image, its magnitude falls off as a power law in frequency:
$$\lVert \mathscr{L}(u,v) \rVert \simeq \frac{1}{ w ^ \alpha}$$
where $w$ denotes the radial spatial frequency ($w = \sqrt{u + v}$), $\mathscr{L}(u,v)$ is the Fourier transform of the image $\ell[n,m]$, and $\alpha \simeq 1$. This property holds across all orientations.

In natural images, the largest amplitudes concentrate in the low spatial frequencies, whereas random images have similar spectral content at all frequencies. By calculating the average magnitude of the FT over all angular directions, it can be seen that the decay along the radial frequency roughly follows a $1/w^{1.5}$ decay in many examples. This property is shared across images despite very distinct appearances.

(see figure: (top) Three natural images with size 512 $\times$ 512 pixels, and one random image. (middle) The magnitude of their Fourier transforms (FT), images are transformed to grayscale by averaging the three...)
concepts.motivation_md: This power-law decay is a universal statistical signature of natural scenes, distinguishing them from random noise and providing a basis for image compression and modeling.
concepts.recap_md:
- Natural images exhibit a characteristic $1/w^\alpha$ decay in their Fourier magnitude.
- This indicates that low-frequency components (coarse structures) dominate over high-frequency components.

concepts.title: Sampling from the Gaussian Model
concepts.one_liner: Images can be sampled from a Gaussian model by specifying a covariance matrix with a power-law power spectrum.
concepts.content:
Once a distribution is defined, it can be used to sample new images. This requires specifying the parameters of the distribution, specifically the covariance matrix ${\bf C}$. Images can be generated using the $1/ w^\alpha$ model to fill the diagonal values of the matrix ${\bf D}$. These images are created by combining a random phase with a power spectrum magnitude following $1/(1+w ^\alpha)$, typically with $\alpha=1.5$. The addition of 1 to the denominator avoids division by zero. This generative process can also be applied to color images by sampling each color channel independently.

(see figure: (top) Images are generated by making an image with a random phase and with a magnitude of the power spectrum following $1/ (1+w ^\alpha)$ with $\alpha=1.5$. (bottom) Same generative process applied...)
concepts.motivation_md: Sampling allows researchers to visualize what features are captured by a statistical model and to verify if the model produces images that look 'natural'.
concepts.recap_md:
- Sampling involves using a random phase and a power-law magnitude in the Fourier domain.
- The parameter $\alpha$ (often 1.5) controls the 'roughness' or frequency decay of the sampled image.

concepts.title: Matching Natural Image Parameters
concepts.one_liner: New images can be sampled by matching the Fourier Transform magnitude of individual natural images while replacing the phase with random noise.
concepts.content:
We can sample new images by matching the parameters of individual natural images. To process color images, we first look for a color space that decorrelates color information for each image. This is achieved by applying principal component analysis (PCA) to the three color channels, resulting in a $3 \times 3$ matrix that produces three decorrelated channels. For each channel, we compute the Fourier Transform (FT), keep the magnitude, and replace the phase with random noise. Finally, we compute the new generated image by performing the inverse FT and applying the inverse of the PCA matrix to return to the original color space. This process results in images that maintain a similar color distribution to the inputs.

(see figure: Examples of images and random samples with the same magnitude of the FT of the corresponding image. We use PCA in color space to find decorrelated color components. Then, each decorrelated color...)
concepts.motivation_md: This technique allows for the generation of synthetic textures or images that share the statistical properties (specifically the power spectrum and color distribution) of a specific reference image, which is useful for studying visual perception and image statistics.
concepts.recap_md:
- Use PCA to decorrelate color channels into a $3 \times 3$ matrix.
 - Keep the FT magnitude of the original image but randomize the phase.
 - Apply the inverse FT and inverse PCA to reconstruct the image in the original color space.

concepts.title: Image Denoising: Wiener Filter
concepts.one_liner: Image denoising under a Gaussian model can be solved using a Wiener filter, which provides a closed-form MAP estimate in both spatial and Fourier domains.
concepts.content:
Image denoising can be formulated using a prior on the correlation structure of natural images. In this problem, we observe a noisy image $\boldsymbol\ell_g$ corrupted with white Gaussian noise: $$\ell_g[n, m] = \ell[n, m] + g[n, m]$$ The goal is to recover the uncorrupted image $\ell[n,m]$, where the noise $g[m, n]$ has variance $\sigma_g^2$. This is formulated as finding the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate: $$\max_{\boldsymbol\ell} p(\boldsymbol\ell\bigm | \boldsymbol\ell_g) = \max_{\boldsymbol\ell} p({\boldsymbol\ell}_g \bigm | {\boldsymbol\ell}) p({\boldsymbol\ell})$$ The likelihood and prior functions are defined as: $$\begin{aligned} p({\boldsymbol\ell}_g \bigm | {\boldsymbol\ell}) & \propto \exp( - \left| {\boldsymbol\ell}_g - {\boldsymbol\ell} ight| ^2 / \sigma_g^2) \\ p({\boldsymbol\ell}) & \propto \exp \left(-\frac{1}{2} {\boldsymbol\ell}^T {\bf C}^{-1} {\boldsymbol\ell} \right) \end{aligned}$$ The closed-form solution is a linear operation: $${\boldsymbol\ell} = {\bf C} \left( {\bf C} + \sigma_g^2 \mathbf{I} \right)^{-1} {\boldsymbol\ell}_g$$ In the Fourier domain, this is expressed as: $$\mathscr{L}(v) = \frac{A/|v|^{2\alpha}}{A/|v|^{2\alpha} + \sigma_g^2} \mathscr{L}_g(v)$$

(see figure: (Top row) Ground truth decomposition of image into Gaussian white noise and the image, uncorrupted by noise. (bottom row) Gaussian image model denoising results. Note that the estimated noise image...)
concepts.motivation_md: The Wiener filter provides an optimal way to recover an image from Gaussian noise by leveraging the known power-law correlation structure of natural images.
concepts.recap_md:
- Formulates denoising as a MAP estimation problem using a Gaussian prior.
 - The solution is a linear operation involving the image covariance matrix.
 - In the Fourier domain, the filter attenuates frequencies based on the signal-to-noise ratio.

concepts.title: Wavelet Marginal Model
concepts.one_liner: The Wavelet Marginal Model extends Gaussian models by using localized filter banks and measuring the histogram shape of filter responses to capture edges and lines.
concepts.content: The Wavelet Marginal Model extends the Gaussian prior to better capture image properties like flat regions, edges, and lines. It does this in two ways: (1) using localized filters (such as Gaussian derivatives, Gabor filters, or steerable pyramids) instead of global sinusoids, and (2) measuring the histogram shape of all filter responses rather than just mean power. For a filter bank of $K$ filters with kernels $h_k [n,m]$, and assuming filter outputs are independent, the prior model for natural images is: $$p(\boldsymbol\ell) = \prod_{k=0}^{K-1} \prod_{n,m} p_k(\ell_k [n,m])$$ This distribution is the product over all filters and locations of the likelihood of each filtered value, where $p_k$ typically follows a generalized Laplacian distribution.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard Gaussian models generate cloud-like images because they only capture correlation; the Wavelet Marginal Model is needed to represent the sparse, localized structures like edges found in real-world scenes.
concepts.recap_md:
- Uses a bank of localized band-pass filters to capture local image structure.
 - Assumes independence between filter outputs to simplify the joint probability.
 - Models the distribution of filter responses using non-Gaussian histograms.

concepts.title: Non-Gaussian Distribution of Filter Responses
concepts.one_liner: Band-pass filtered natural images exhibit a characteristic non-Gaussian distribution with a sharp peak at zero and heavy tails.
concepts.content:
When natural images are processed with band-pass filters, such as image derivatives or Gabor filters, the resulting output follows a non-Gaussian distribution. While the histogram of an unfiltered image lacks a consistent structure across different images, the histograms of filter outputs (like horizontal or vertical derivatives) are remarkably clean, symmetric, and have a unique maximum around zero. This observation contradicts the Gaussian image model; if the Gaussian model were correct, any linear operation like filtering would result in a Gaussian output. Instead, natural images produce highly kurtotic distributions when filtered.

(see figure: (a) Input image. (b) Horizontal and (c) vertical derivatives of the input image. (d) Histogram of pixel intensities of the input image. (e and f) Histograms of the two derivatives of the original...)

(see figure: Comparison of histograms of images from different visual worlds, and band-pass filtered versions of those images. (top row) Gaussian noise. Band-pass filtered Gaussian noise is still Gaussian...)
concepts.motivation_md: Recognizing that filter responses are non-Gaussian is crucial for building more accurate statistical models of images, as it reveals the sparse nature of edges and details in natural scenes.
concepts.recap_md:
- Band-pass filter outputs of natural images are non-Gaussian and symmetric.
 - These distributions typically feature a sharp peak at zero, representing sparse features.
 - This property distinguishes natural images from pure Gaussian noise models.

concepts.title: Generalized Laplacian Distribution
concepts.one_liner: The generalized Laplacian distribution parameterizes the non-Gaussian outputs of band-pass filters using shape and scale parameters.
concepts.content:
The distribution of intensity values in an image filtered by a band-pass filter $h$ can be parameterized by the generalized Laplacian distribution: $$p(\ell_h[n,m] = x) = \frac{\exp \left(- \left| x/s \right|^r \right)}{2 (s/r) \Gamma(1/r)}$$ This distribution has two parameters: the exponent $r$, which determines the shape, and the scale parameter $s$, which influences variance. In natural images, $r$ typically lies between $0.4$ and $0.8$. Special cases include $r=2$ (Gaussian), $r=1$ (standard Laplacian), $r \to \infty$ (uniform distribution), and $r \to 0$ (delta function).

(see figure: Generalized Laplacian distribution with $s=1$ and (a) $r=0.1$, (b) $r=1$, (c) $r=2$, and (d) $r=10$. %Changing the exponent $r$ changes the shape of the distribution, generating some special case...)
concepts.motivation_md: This distribution provides a flexible mathematical framework to model the heavy-tailed, sparse nature of image derivatives, which is essential for tasks like denoising and inpainting.
concepts.recap_md:
- Parameterizes filter responses using shape $r$ and scale $s$.
 - Natural images typically exhibit $r < 1$, indicating a highly kurtotic (sparse) distribution.
 - It generalizes the Gaussian ($r=2$) and Laplacian ($r=1$) distributions.

concepts.title: Toy Model of Image Inpainting Derivation
concepts.one_liner: The optimal value for a missing pixel depends on the shape parameter $r$ of the image prior, with $r < 1$ favoring sharp edges.
concepts.motivation_md: This derivation demonstrates why non-Gaussian priors ($r < 1$) are superior for image restoration tasks like inpainting, as they correctly preserve sharp boundaries instead of blurring them.
concepts.recap_md:
- Gaussian priors ($r=2$) result in smooth, averaged interpolations.
 - Sparse priors ($r < 1$) favor sharp edges by choosing values that minimize the number of non-zero derivatives.
 - The transition in behavior occurs at $r=1$.

concepts.title: Bayesian Image Denoising
concepts.one_liner: Bayesian image denoising uses the heavy-tailed distribution of filter responses as a prior to estimate true coefficients from noisy observations.
concepts.content:
The highly kurtotic distribution of band-pass filter responses provides a regularity useful for image denoising. Assuming additive Gaussian noise with variance $\sigma^2$, the likelihood of a true coefficient $x$ given an observed noisy coefficient $\hat{x}$ is: $$p(\hat{x} \bigm | x) \propto \exp{ \left( -\frac{(x - �\hat{x})^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right) }$$ Using a Laplacian prior ($r=1$) for the subbands, $p(x) \propto \exp{ \left( -\frac{\left| x \right|}{s} \right) }$, the posterior probability is: $$P(x \bigm | \hat{x}) \propto \exp{ \left( -\frac{\left| x \right|}{s} \right)} \exp{ \left( -\frac{(x - \hat{x})^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right) }$$ This Bayesian approach allows for estimating the true coefficient value. For small observed values, the posterior peak remains at zero, effectively shrinking noise toward zero, while larger observations yield estimates closer to the observed value.

(see figure: Showing the likelihood, prior, and posterior terms for the estimation of a subband coefficient from several noisy observations. (a) A zero subband coefficient is observed. (b) An observation of 0.26...)
concepts.motivation_md: By combining a Gaussian noise model with a sparse Laplacian prior, we can more effectively distinguish between actual image features (which are sparse) and noise (which is pervasive).
concepts.recap_md:
- Combines a Gaussian likelihood (noise) with a Laplacian prior (image structure).
 - The posterior distribution determines the most likely original coefficient.
 - This method naturally performs 'shrinkage,' where small noisy coefficients are suppressed toward zero.

slots.example:
The highly kurtotic distribution of band-pass filter responses provides a regularity useful for image denoising. Assuming additive Gaussian noise with variance $\sigma^2$, the likelihood of a true coefficient $x$ given an observed noisy coefficient $\hat{x}$ is: $$p(\hat{x} \bigm | x) \propto \exp{ \left( -\frac{(x - �\hat{x})^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right) }$$ Using a Laplacian prior ($r=1$) for the subbands, $p(x) \propto \exp{ \left( -\frac{\left| x \right|}{s} \right) }$, the posterior probability is: $$P(x \bigm | \hat{x}) \propto \exp{ \left( -\frac{\left| x \right|}{s} \right)} \exp{ \left( -\frac{(x - \hat{x})^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right) }$$ This Bayesian approach allows for estimating the true coefficient value. For small observed values, the posterior peak remains at zero, effectively shrinking noise toward zero, while larger observations yield estimates closer to the observed value.

concepts.title: Laplacian Image Prior
concepts.one_liner: The Laplacian image prior models the probability of subband coefficients using an exponential function of their absolute values.
concepts.content: The prior probability of any subband coefficient value $x$ in a natural image can be modeled using the Laplacian distribution (the generalized Laplacian with $r=1$): $$p(x) \propto \exp{ \left( -\frac{\left| x \right|}{s} \right) }$$ This prior reflects the observation that most filter responses in natural images are near zero, with occasional large values corresponding to edges.
concepts.motivation_md: The Laplacian prior is a mathematically convenient way to enforce sparsity in image representations, which is a fundamental property of natural scenes.
concepts.recap_md:
- Assumes a shape parameter of $r=1$ in the generalized Laplacian model.
 - Represents the sparse distribution of edges and features in images.
 - Used as a prior in Bayesian estimation and denoising.

prereq.rationale: Sampling as a technique for model assessment is demonstrated specifically using the independent pixel model.
Both procedural and statistical models are developed specifically to represent the unique properties of natural images/photographs.
The power law describes the specific mathematical decay of the power spectrum (or FT magnitude) across frequencies in natural images.
The Gaussian image model is a maximum entropy distribution derived by using the pixel correlation function as the primary constraint.
The Gaussian model is designed to account for the power spectrum statistics observed in natural images.
Sampling from the Gaussian model requires the distribution parameters, specifically the covariance matrix defined in the model.
Denoising with a Wiener filter uses the Gaussian model as a prior for the correlation structure of the image.
The problem assumes the image is corrupted by additive white Gaussian noise.
The concept of statistical regularities is fundamentally about defining the boundaries and constraints of the 'natural image' manifold.
This idea builds on the definition of statistical models as those that operate on low-level data without semantic understanding.
The Wavelet Marginal Model is explicitly introduced as an extension of the Gaussian prior to better account for the non-Gaussian statistics of natural images.
The derivation specifically calculates the probability of a signal under the wavelet marginal model to find optimal missing values.
The denoising process uses the heavy-tailed statistics of filter responses, parameterized by the generalized Laplacian, as a prior for the true signal.
The denoising derivation assumes the observed signal is corrupted by additive Gaussian noise.
The Efros and Leung algorithm directly exploits the Markov property of images for texture synthesis.
The weighting function is the mechanism that determines which pixels are averaged in the nonlocal means algorithm.
Visual worlds are defined as simplifications of natural images, making an understanding of natural images a prerequisite.

overlay.rationale: The independent pixel model is presented as the simplest form of a statistical image model.
Both concepts treat images as collections of independent pixels whose global intensity distribution is the primary object of study.
The perceptual changes in material appearance demonstrate the practical significance of histogram matching and manipulation.
This definition formalizes the 'stationary noise' concept used to differentiate noise from surface texture.
The dead leaves model is a prime example of a procedural model (defined by a generation process) used to approximate statistical properties of natural images.
Unlike the independent pixel model, the Gaussian model accounts for the spatial correlation between different pixels.
This technique concretely demonstrates how to generate images using the 1/w^alpha power-law observed in natural images.
Both are techniques for generating new images by manipulating statistical or spectral parameters.
Sampling is the standard test for whether a model has successfully captured the regularities of the target distribution.
Denoising is explicitly cited as a primary application of capturing these statistical regularities.
Image synthesis is explicitly cited as a primary application of capturing these statistical regularities.
The Gaussian model is a prime example of a 'simple model' that captures some regularities but fails to sample realistic natural images.
The observation of highly kurtotic filter outputs contradicts the Gaussian model, which predicts that any linear operation on a Gaussian signal remains Gaussian.
The generalized Laplacian provides a mathematical formula to parameterize the specific shape (sharp peak and heavy tails) observed in filtered natural images.
The derivation shows how different values of the shape parameter r in the generalized Laplacian lead to either smooth (r>1) or sharp (r<1) reconstructions.
The Laplacian prior is defined as the specific instance of the generalized Laplacian distribution where the shape parameter r is set to 1.
The coring function is the practical mapping derived from the MAP estimation process in Bayesian denoising, showing how small values are suppressed.
MRFs generalize the independent pixel model by allowing local dependencies between neighboring pixels.
Unlike MRFs which assume local dependencies, nonlocal means denoising aggregates information from all pixels in the image.
Nonlocal means is a patch-based denoising technique, contrasting with the Wiener filter's LSI approach based on power spectra.
Nonlocal means is a modern alternative to the Bayesian denoising techniques discussed in previous sections.
Nonlocal means denoising shares the intuition of using neighborhood similarity with the Efros and Leung synthesis algorithm.
